entry.evidence: an understanding of how snow surface topography affects snow albedo is imperative

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), with PDF for figure pages

steps.action: Frame the question of how snow surface topography makes apparent and intrinsic albedo diverge, a distinction the authors say is often ignored.
steps.quote: an understanding of how snow surface topography affects snow albedo is imperative

steps.action: Take from the literature the expectation that models lacking within-field-of-view illumination variation are biased high, and Warren et al.'s two roughness mechanisms (illumination angle, photon trapping).
steps.quote: the widely used albedo models cited above do not account for varying illumination within the field of view

steps.action: Build and characterize the radiometer setup: a self-leveling adjustable arm kept about 1 m above the snow, a height chosen by experiment to minimize field-of-view and shadow artifacts; PSPs and an SPN1 for the diffuse ratio.
steps.quote: By experiment, we found that the combination of these two artifacts is minimized when the radiometer is ∼ 1 m above the snow

steps.action: Check the irradiance measurements against SMARTS modeled irradiance (Fig. 2, Table 1).
steps.quote: The comparison between SMARTS and the measurements yields R 2 ≥ 0 .99 for both the PSP and the SPN1

steps.action: Compare reflected radiation from the fixed and adjustable arms across deep, patchy and snow-free conditions (Fig. 3) to show non-snow contamination, then use only the adjustable-arm radiometers.
steps.quote: the downlooking radiometers on the adjustable boom have greater values than those on the fixed arm

steps.action: Scan the snow surface hourly with an automated terrestrial laser scanner over the 2021 water year, filter the point clouds, and grid them to 1 cm surfaces masked to the radiometer footprint.
steps.quote: A Riegl VZ-400 laser scanner automatically scanned the snow surface every hour during the 2021 water year.

steps.action: Develop the spatial albedo model: point-wise illumination angles, view factors and horizons, an order-of-scattering treatment of multiple reflections, and an empirical function from SMARTS and Warren (1982) simulations for wavelength-integrated albedo after each reflection (Fig. 4).
steps.quote: we derive an empirical function to estimate intrinsic broadband and near-infrared albedos at step n

steps.action: Obtain Sentinel-2 L2A surface reflectance for a flat, nearly fully snow-covered target pixel 2.2 km from CUES; convert it to broadband albedo and process it with SPIReS.
steps.quote: Bottom-of-atmosphere (surface, Level 2A) reflectance estimates from the Sentinel-2A/B (S2) multispectral instrument were obtained.

steps.action: Estimate the S2 broadband albedo uncertainty from repeat acquisitions over a bare-ground reference pixel and compare it with a published S2 validation.
steps.quote: Broadband albedo uncertainty from S2 (0.036) was estimated based on maximum differences between acquisitions for a bare-ground target pixel

steps.action: Measure in situ spectral reflectance with a field spectrometer and a Spectralon panel on clear days.
steps.quote: A Spectra Vista HR-1024i was used with a Spectralon panel with 0.99 albedo

steps.action: Infer daily intrinsic albedo by matching the modeled spatial albedo to the measured uncorrected albedo, giving a seasonal time series with mean intrinsic-minus-apparent differences (Fig. 6).
steps.quote: the differences amounted to - 0.056 in the broadband albedo and - 0.052 in the near infrared

steps.action: Compare the result with earlier shorter studies: the sign agrees, and the magnitude exceeds the Larue et al. (2020) estimate.
steps.quote: agreeing with previous work over more limited timespans

steps.action: Estimate the photon-trapping share of the radiation lost (mean 4 % broadband, 5 % NIR, over 20 % in late spring).
steps.quote: characterizes photon trapping, which accounts for a mean of 4 % of the lost broadband radiation

steps.action: Compare planar-corrected with intrinsic albedo to show the previous planar correction captures slope but not sub-slope roughness, and draw implications for terrain correction by sensor resolution.
steps.quote: accounts for surface slope but not for roughness

steps.action: Compare S2 narrow-to-broadband albedo with CUES uncorrected albedo (Fig. 7) to show satellites see the apparent albedo.
steps.quote: Narrow-to-broadband albedo conversions confirm that the apparent albedo is being seen from space.

steps.action: State rival causes of darkening (impurities vs. shade from roughness) with distinct spectral signatures, and hypothesize that sufficient spectral resolution separates them.
steps.quote: an instrument with sufficient spectral resolution and accuracy should be able to discriminate between the causes of darkening

steps.action: Design the test: run SPIReS on S2 imagery under a dirty-snow and a clean-snow assumption, both with a shade endmember, and unmix field-spectrometer spectra.
steps.quote: [...] hypothesis, SPIReS was run on S2 imagery with dirty snow endmembers and with a clean snow assumption.

steps.action: Invert for grain size, dust concentration, fsca and fshade from S2 (dirty and clean runs) and from SVC spectra (Table 2, Fig. 9).
steps.quote: In the clean-snow run, the dust endmember is swapped for the shade endmember (Table 2).

steps.action: Compare the solutions: S2 albedos under both assumptions are indistinguishable within error, while spectrometer solutions consistently separate shade from dust (Fig. 8, Fig. 9).
steps.quote: With overlapping error bars for each scene, the resulting albedos are indistinguishable within measured error

steps.action: Compute with radiative transfer simulations how the intrinsic-apparent difference depends on shade fraction across grain sizes, zenith angles and impurities (Fig. 10).
steps.quote: Figure 10 shows the results of radiative transfer simulations to illustrate the effect of shade on the difference between intrinsic and apparent albedo.

steps.action: Update the Bair et al. (2019) lookup tables and albedo model to output apparent albedo as a function of fshade (Eq. 10).
steps.quote: the lookup tables and albedo model presented in Bair et al. (2019) have been updated to include f shade

steps.action: Keep the claims: intrinsic exceeds apparent albedo by a quantified amount; multispectral sensors confuse roughness darkening with low impurity loads; shade must be included in unmixing and albedo models.
steps.quote: the results show that intrinsic albedo is consistently greater than apparent albedo

steps.action: Referee 1 called the apparent/intrinsic definitions non-standard; authors clarified that roughness covers slope, aspect and view factor, and the published definition cites Nicodemus et al. and Schaepman-Strub et al.

steps.action: Authors revised the roughness-feature paragraphs using Filhol and Sturm (2015), corrected the sastrugi statements, and added Wright et al. (2014).

steps.action: Both referees questioned the San Juan dust properties and 3 µm radius; authors justified them in the rebuttal (SNICAR's western U.S. dust, their own measured samples) without new runs.
steps.page: RC1 ¶17; RC2 ¶9; AC1-S p.4; AC2-S p.2
steps.quote: We use the optical properties of the San Juan dust and solve for the mass concentration for each day.

steps.action: Referee 1 suggested lidar surveys over the satellite target pixel; authors declined because the scanner is not portable.
steps.quote: Probably not. The lidar is not really portable

steps.action: Referee 2 asked how slope and aspect, the mask, B and D, and the spatial mean albedo are computed; authors clarified the 1 cm DEM treatment, the footprint mask, the measured diffuse ratio, and the spatial mean.
steps.quote: We treat the rough surface in a similar way that we would consider a digital elevation model (DEM) over mountainous terrain

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for a figure of the illumination angle; authors declined, saying the equation is standard.
steps.quote: We can, although this equation for illumination angle is standard.

steps.action: Referee 2 asked what sets the x-axis spread in Fig. 4 and why the increase peaks at 0.68-0.80; authors added grain size and impurity range to the caption but only speculated on the peak.
steps.quote: The spread in the x-axis covers the range of values of the intrinsic albedo we encountered during the experiment

steps.action: Referee 2 asked how often and why the adjustable arm was moved; authors added the two-artifact rationale and the ~1 m height found by experiment (now §2.1 ¶1).
steps.quote: By experiment, we found that the combination of these two artifacts is minimized when the radiometer is ~1 m above the snow

end.claim: Over 110 days of the 2021 season at CUES, intrinsic albedo exceeded apparent albedo by a mean of 0.056 broadband and 0.052 near-infrared (0.022 after a planar correction), a darkening multispectral sensors cannot distinguish from low impurity concentrations.

decisive_move.sentence: The spatial albedo model, which uses hourly 1 cm lidar topography to compute illumination, view factors and multiple reflections and then solves for intrinsic albedo, is what makes the seasonal intrinsic-apparent difference exist as a number.

gates.evidence: The lidar and radiometer records come from automated year-round monitoring at CUES, directed by the question of roughness effects rather than by a stated hypothesis. The spectral-discrimination hypothesis (§3 ¶6) is stated after the data and tested by the dirty/clean SPIReS swap and the spectrometer unmixing (§3 ¶7–¶8), a test that could have failed. The headline 0.056 estimate faced no failable test beyond agreement in sign with earlier studies (§3 ¶3). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Simple morphological filter for removing the arm from lidar point clouds (Pingel et al., 2013)
Radiometer footprint of about 8.7h for 95 % of reflected radiation (Sailor et al., 2006)
Shade endmember in spectral mixture modeling (Adams et al., 1986, Viking Lander site)
Mie scattering coupled to two-stream radiative transfer

novelty_claims.quote: none of these studies have tracked the snow surface topography throughout a snow season
nor have they examined the effects of snow surface topography on [...]
To our knowledge, CUES is the only site where snow albedo is measured using an adjustable albedo arm.

limits:
Composition none_fits: this is a single-site, single-season measurement-and-estimation case study, with a nested hypothesis test added in the discussion. Conditions are found and repeat daily, but no regularity is fitted across the repetitions, and no rival set is excluded by a crucial test.

Sub-claim statuses:
- The headline difference (0.056 broadband, 0.052 NIR, 0.022 after planar correction) is estimate_with_resolution, but no uncertainty is reported for the mean difference itself.
- 'Multispectral sensors cannot separate shade from low dust' is best_explanation, resting on a few S2 scenes and a single 11 May 2021 comparison (Table 2).
- 'The field spectrometer discriminates shade from dust' is best_explanation from a few SVC spectra with large spatial variability.
- The recommendations (always use a shade endmember; models should output apparent albedo; terrain-correction caution at ≤30 m) are inferences, not tested here.

Untested assumptions and choices:
- The spatial model is not tested for sensitivity to grid resolution, dust optical properties, the Lambertian assumption, or the number of reflections.
- The S2 target pixel is 2.2 km away and is assumed to share CUES snow conditions.
- The 1 m arm height was set 'by experiment', and that experiment is not reported.

Record inconsistencies:
- The published §3 ¶2 still says 'the surface roughness (in degrees, divided by 30 for scale) is plotted', although the authors told referees they would remove this quantity and the published Fig. 7 caption omits it. Inference: an incomplete revision.
- The rebuttal attributes the Fig. 2 offset possibly to water vapor in SMARTS; the published caption attributes it to thermal responses. Neither was tested.

The review file shows no request for new analyses and no failed attempts; the paper reports no abandoned approaches.

disagreements.target: Widely used snow albedo models (Warren 1982 lineage; Bair et al. 2019; Flanner et al. 2021; Gardner and Sharp 2010)
disagreements.support: The seasonal estimate shows intrinsic albedo exceeds apparent albedo by 0.056 on average, so models that output intrinsic albedo are biased high for rough snow.
disagreements.quote: the widely used albedo models cited above do not account for varying illumination within the field of view, meaning their results can be positively biased

disagreements.target: Multi-angle and sub-pixel roughness approaches (Corbett and Su 2015; Kuchiki et al. 2011; Lyapustin et al. 2010; Nolin and Payne [...]
disagreements.support: Argument only: midlatitude snow cover changes between overpasses and pixels are mixed; no test is offered.
disagreements.quote: ill-suited towards dynamic midlatitude snowpacks with mixed pixels

disagreements.target: Albedo measurements at other tower sites (Elder et al. 2009; Landry et al. 2014; Lejeune et al. 2019; Lhermitte et [...]
disagreements.support: Examination of published tower images plus the fixed-vs-adjustable arm comparison (Fig. 3), which shows non-snow objects lower measured albedo.
disagreements.quote: [...] non-snow objects within the downlooking radiometer's field of view at every site

disagreements.target: Larue et al. (2020) roughness-induced albedo decrease of -0.02 to -0.03
disagreements.support: The seasonal difference with extensive ablation hollows is -0.056 broadband and -0.052 NIR.
disagreements.quote: in the snow studied here with extensive ablation hollows, the magnitudes are greater

disagreements.target: Planar terrain correction used in previous research (Bair et al. 2018; Painter et al. 2012b)
disagreements.support: Intrinsic albedo is generally greater than planar-corrected albedo (Fig. 6c), with a mean residual of 0.022.
disagreements.quote: planar correction that has been performed in previous research (Bair et al., 2018; Painter et al., 2012b) accounts for surface slope

disagreements.target: Energy balance models that use intrinsic albedo
disagreements.support: The quantified divergence and the updated model producing apparent albedo from fshade.
disagreements.quote: The apparent albedo produced should be used in energy balance models where intrinsic albedos have been previously used.
